title: The Reproducible Analysis Record
lede: Every physics claim about the breeder (Hyperion) traces to one of 81 versioned analyses that regenerate from source, so a reader can reproduce the number, not just read it.
body: The breeder (Hyperion) is a compact D-T spherical tokamak studied in simulation. Its design point is not a slide deck of round numbers; it is a set of 81 analyses that each take fixed inputs, run defined code, and emit a defined output. The headline figures — scientific gain Q_sci of 3.076, fusion power of 85.0 MW, plasma current of 9.66 MA, peak field of 16.84 T with 8 T on-axis — are outputs of those analyses, not assertions layered on top of them.

An analysis is reproducible when a third party, given the inputs and the code, obtains the same output within a stated tolerance. Each of the 81 carries its inputs, the exact code revision, a random seed where stochastic, and an expected output. The record is regenerated end-to-end rather than hand-edited, so a changed input propagates to every figure that depends on it and cannot silently disagree with the text.
Why it is structured this way

A fusion design claim is only as good as the ability of someone else to check it. Publishing prose without the underlying computation asks the reader to trust the author. Publishing the computation asks the reader to trust arithmetic they can rerun. Kronos chose the second posture across the whole breeder program, and the same discipline governs the open honest gates: the tritium-breeding-ratio reconciliation and the center-post lifetime are recorded as open items, not smoothed over.

This page describes a design-and-simulation study, not a built machine. Construction of the breeder (Hyperion) begins Q2 2027; first-of-a-kind first tritium is targeted near 2030. No hardware net-gain claim is made before FOAK.

title: What Is Simulated vs What Is Demonstrated
lede: Hyperion is entirely a design-and-simulation study today; nothing here is hardware-demonstrated, and the record labels every claim with which of those two it is.
body: A hard line between the two

There is a category difference between a number that came out of a code and a number that came out of a machine. The breeder (Hyperion) program is, at this date, on the simulated side of that line for every quantity. The value of stating this plainly is that it tells a reader exactly how much weight each figure can bear.

Everything: the equilibrium and its negative triangularity of delta -0.30, the confinement and gain estimate, the neutron budget, the breeding blanket behavior, and the product yields near 4 kg/yr tritium class plus 1.97 kg/yr helium-3. These are computed from models with stated assumptions and stated uncertainties.

Nothing, in the sense of full-system fusion hardware. Individual technologies (REBCO conductor, vacuum systems) exist in industry, but the integrated breeder has not been built. First-of-a-kind first tritium near 2030 is the first hardware event that will move specific claims from the left column to the right. Until then, the honest reading of every headline number is: this is what the model says the machine should do.

The line is not permanent. It is a ledger that FOAK begins to move, entry by entry, as measurement replaces prediction. The purpose of drawing it sharply now is so that later movement is legible: when a quantity crosses from simulated to demonstrated, the record can say exactly which one and on what evidence, instead of a vague overall claim of progress.

title: The Honest Gates, Stated Plainly
lede: The breeder record names the open physics questions it has not closed — chiefly the tritium-breeding-ratio reconciliation and the center-post lifetime — rather than presenting a finished machine.
body: A design study that reports only its successes is not a validation record; it is advertising. The breeder (Hyperion) program states its open gates as findings of equal standing to its results. Three are load-bearing for the breeder specifically.

Local-vs-net tritium breeding ratio: at the target TBR of 1.8, the reconciliation between an idealized local breeding figure and a realistic net figure (blanket coverage, penetrations, losses) is open.
Tritium self-sufficiency: not yet proven. The machine must breed more tritium than it burns plus decay and process losses, and that closure is a design target, not a demonstrated fact.

Center-post lifetime: the compact spherical-tokamak center stack sits in a hard neutron field; a limited-lifetime note (order 0.01 full-power-years for the most exposed element) is recorded as an engineering constraint, not waved away.

title: The Published Papers and Their DOIs
lede: The breeder analysis is deposited publicly on Zenodo with citable DOIs, so the record has a permanent address independent of any Kronos-controlled website.
body: The breeder (Hyperion) design-and-simulation record is deposited on Zenodo, an open repository operated by CERN. A Zenodo deposit has a persistent DOI, a fixed content hash, and a public landing page that does not depend on Kronos infrastructure. If this website disappeared, the record would remain.
A version-independent concept DOI resolves to the latest version so a citation never goes stale.

<svg viewBox="0 0 600 190" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="publication path" style="width:100%;height:auto;max-width:640px;display:block;margin:14px 0;background:#232C39;border:1px solid #D4AD5C;border-radius:8px"><rect x="20" y="60" width="125" height="70" rx="6" fill="#2c3745" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="82" y="95" fill="#e6e9ee" font-family="monospace" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">author analysis</text><line x1="148" y1="95" x2="162" y2="95" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M162 95 l -6 -4 l 0 8 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="165" y="60" width="125" height="70" rx="6" fill="#2c3745" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="227" y="95" fill="#e6e9ee" font-family="monospace" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">deposit to Zenodo</text><line x1="293" y1="95" x2="307" y2="95" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M307 95 l -6 -4 l 0 8 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="310" y="60" width="125" height="70" rx="6" fill="#2c3745" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="372" y="95" fill="#e6e9ee" font-family="monospace" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">DOI minted</text><line x1="438" y1="95" x2="452" y2="95" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M452 95 l -6 -4 l 0 8 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="455" y="60" width="125" height="70" rx="6" fill="#2c3745" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="517" y="87" fill="#e6e9ee" font-family="monospace" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">anyone cites &</text><text x="517" y="102" fill="#e6e9ee" font-family="monospace" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">fetches</text></svg>
What a DOI does and does not guarantee

A DOI guarantees that a specific set of files is permanently retrievable and unambiguously named. It does not, by itself, guarantee peer review or correctness. Those are separate processes. The DOI is the anchor that lets peer review, reproduction, and correction all point at exactly the same bytes.

Depositing externally also removes a conflict of interest from the record's permanence. A claim hosted only on a company site can be edited or withdrawn by that company; a Zenodo deposit cannot be altered without leaving a public version record. For a program asking to be taken on the strength of its openness, putting the primary record beyond its own reach is the point, not a technicality.

Cite the version DOI when a claim depends on a specific number, so the reference is unambiguous even after later corrections. Cite the concept DOI when referring to the breeder work in general. See How to Cite Hyperion for exact formats.

title: Inside the Zenodo Deposit
lede: The breeder deposit is not a single PDF; it bundles the paper, the analysis inputs, the code revision, and the checksums needed to verify and rerun it.
body: The breeder (Hyperion) Zenodo deposit is organized so that reading and reproducing are both possible from the same download. A reader who only wants the argument reads the manuscript; a reader who wants to check a number opens the corresponding analysis.
The manuscript, describing the design point, methods, results, and the open gates.
Frozen inputs for each of the 81 analyses, with units and provenance.
The code revision (or a pinned reference to it) that turns inputs into outputs.
Expected outputs and tolerances, so a rerun can be judged pass or fail.
Checksums for every file, so a download can be verified byte-for-byte.

Each deposit carries a manifest listing every file and its hash. A reader computes the hashes locally and compares; a mismatch means the download is corrupt or altered. This is the mechanism that makes two-tier reproduction possible: a Tier-1 byte-exact check and a Tier-2 within-tolerance check.
The breeder deposit is a physics and engineering record. It contains no prices, no financial projections, and no cost figures. Product quantities are stated in mass and neutron terms only.

title: Versioning the Record
lede: The breeder record moved from v1 to a corrected v2 in the open; both DOIs remain resolvable, so the correction is visible rather than hidden.
body: When the breeder (Hyperion) analysis was corrected, the fix was published as a new Zenodo version with its own DOI (10.5281/zenodo.21795620) rather than by overwriting the first (10.5281/zenodo.21746157). Both versions stay online. Anyone who cited v1 can still retrieve exactly what they cited, and anyone comparing the two can see precisely what changed.

<svg viewBox="0 0 600 190" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="version history" style="width:100%;height:auto;max-width:640px;display:block;margin:14px 0;background:#232C39;border:1px solid #D4AD5C;border-radius:8px"><rect x="20" y="60" width="125" height="70" rx="6" fill="#2c3745" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="82" y="95" fill="#e6e9ee" font-family="monospace" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">v1 deposited</text><line x1="148" y1="95" x2="162" y2="95" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M162 95 l -6 -4 l 0 8 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="165" y="60" width="125" height="70" rx="6" fill="#2c3745" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="227" y="95" fill="#e6e9ee" font-family="monospace" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">issue found</text><line x1="293" y1="95" x2="307" y2="95" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M307 95 l -6 -4 l 0 8 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="310" y="60" width="125" height="70" rx="6" fill="#2c3745" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="372" y="95" fill="#e6e9ee" font-family="monospace" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">v2 corrected</text><line x1="438" y1="95" x2="452" y2="95" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M452 95 l -6 -4 l 0 8 Z" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="455" y="60" width="125" height="70" rx="6" fill="#2c3745" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="517" y="87" fill="#e6e9ee" font-family="monospace" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">both remain</text><text x="517" y="102" fill="#e6e9ee" font-family="monospace" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle">online</text></svg>

Silently editing a published record breaks reproducibility: a reader who reran v1 last month and a reader who fetches it today would get different files under the same reference. Immutable versions with a linear history make the record trustworthy across time. The concept DOI always points at the newest version for readers who want current numbers.

This discipline has a cost worth naming: the record accumulates versions rather than presenting a single clean document, and a casual reader must choose which to cite. The program accepts that trade because the alternative — a tidy record that silently changed — is exactly the failure that destroys trust in a design study. A visible correction history is a feature of the record, not clutter to be swept away.
The reason for the new version, in plain language.
Which analyses and which figures changed.
Whether any headline number moved, and by how much.
A pointer from the old version to the new.
This mirrors the errata and corrections policy: nothing is removed without a trace, and no correction is presented as if the original were never published.

title: Benchmarking Against Tokamak Databases
lede: The breeder design point is checked against established empirical tokamak scalings and databases, so its numbers sit inside a body of measured experience rather than standing alone.
body: Anchoring a design in measured data

A fusion model can be internally consistent and still disagree with reality. The guard against that is benchmarking: comparing the breeder (Hyperion) design point to empirical scalings derived from decades of tokamak operation. Where the design lands inside the validated range, confidence rises; where it lands at or beyond an edge, the record says so.

The design is compared against the ITER-basis energy-confinement scaling, the Troyon normalized-beta limit, the Greenwald density limit, neoclassical bootstrap-current estimates, and the spherical-tokamak-specific record from machines in the NSTX and MAST class. Each comparison is one or more of the 81 analyses, with the reference law and its stated range of validity cited.

A compact spherical tokamak at aspect ratio 2.5 and R0 1.2 m sits at the edge of where some conventional scalings were fitted. The record does not pretend a scaling law validated at conventional aspect ratio transfers unchanged to low aspect ratio; it flags such extrapolations as assumptions to be tested at FOAK.

Benchmarking is a triangulation, not a single verdict. Confinement, beta, density, and bootstrap current each constrain the design from a different direction, and a point that sits comfortably inside all of them at once is far better supported than one that clears each limit in isolation. The value of the exercise is in the joint picture, which is why the benchmark analyses are read together rather than one at a time.

title: The Confinement Scaling Benchmark
lede: Hyperion's energy-confinement estimate is compared to the ITER-basis H-mode scaling, with an explicit note that low aspect ratio pushes the fit beyond much of its source data.
body: The scientific gain of the breeder (Hyperion), Q_sci 3.076, rests on how well the plasma retains energy — the energy confinement time. The community's standard empirical reference is the ITER-basis H-mode scaling, commonly written IPB98(y,2), fitted to a multi-machine database. The breeder analysis compares its predicted confinement time to that scaling as one of the 81 analyses.

# Illustrative form of the ITER-basis H-mode scaling (IPB98(y,2))
# tau_E ~ 0.0562 * Ip^0.93 * B^0.15 * P^-0.69 * n^0.41
#              * M^0.19 * R^1.97 * eps^0.58 * kappa^0.78
# Ip[MA], B[T], P[MW], n[1e19 m^-3], R[m], eps=a/R, kappa=elongation
# The breeder benchmark evaluates this at the design point and
# compares tau_E to the transport-model prediction used for Q_sci.

At plasma current 9.66 MA and 8 T on-axis, the design point is evaluated against the scaling. The comparison is reported as a ratio of predicted to scaling-implied confinement, with the confidence interval of the scaling propagated through.

IPB98(y,2) was fitted largely at conventional aspect ratio. The breeder runs at A 2.5, low aspect ratio, where spherical tokamaks are known to differ. The record therefore treats the conventional scaling as a cross-check, not as ground truth, and weights the ST-specific database more heavily for confinement inference.

This is where the confinement prediction is most exposed, and the record says so directly. A scaling extrapolated beyond its fitted aspect ratio can be optimistic or pessimistic, and only measurement resolves which. The breeder therefore pre-registers a confinement prediction with an explicit falsifier so the extrapolation is put to a decisive test at FOAK rather than defended by argument.

title: Benchmarking Against the Spherical-Tokamak Database
lede: Because Hyperion is a low-aspect-ratio machine, its confinement and stability estimates are weighted against the NSTX/MAST-class record, not only conventional-tokamak scalings.
body: The breeder (Hyperion) is a spherical tokamak: aspect ratio A 2.5, major radius R0 1.2 m, strong elongation, and negative triangularity delta -0.30. Its natural comparison class is the family of spherical tokamaks — machines in the NSTX and MAST lineage — whose operating record differs from conventional tokamaks in confinement, stability, and current drive.

Existing spherical tokamaks are pulsed research devices, not steady D-T breeders, and none has operated with the breeder's high-temperature-superconducting field or its blanket. The database constrains the plasma physics; it says little about integrated breeding or center-post survival. The record is explicit that the ST benchmark bounds the plasma claims and not the engineering gates.

The comparison is also asymmetric in maturity: several spherical tokamaks have logged extensive campaigns, so the plasma-physics inference rests on real operating hours, while the breeding and center-post questions have no operating analogue at all. The record keeps those two confidence levels separate rather than letting the well-supported plasma benchmark lend borrowed credibility to the unsupported engineering gates.

title: The Beta-Limit Benchmark
lede: The breeder's normalized pressure is checked against the Troyon beta limit, the empirical ceiling on how much plasma pressure a given field and current can hold.
body: How much pressure the field can hold

Fusion power scales steeply with plasma pressure, so a design is tempted toward high beta — the ratio of plasma pressure to magnetic pressure. The empirical ceiling is the Troyon limit, expressed through normalized beta, beta_N. Exceeding it invites large-scale instability. The breeder (Hyperion) design point is checked against this limit as part of the 81-analysis record.

# Troyon normalized-beta limit
# beta[%] <= beta_N * Ip[MA] / (a[m] * B[T])
# beta_N ~ 2.8-4 (conventional); STs access higher values.
# Design inputs: Ip = 9.66 MA, B_axis = 8 T, low aspect ratio.
# The benchmark reports the design beta_N and its margin to the limit.

Low-aspect-ratio machines are known to reach higher beta_N than conventional tokamaks, so the breeder benchmark uses the ST-appropriate range rather than the textbook conventional value. The reported quantity is the design's beta_N together with the margin between it and the applicable limit.

A comfortable margin means the design is not relying on operating at the ragged edge of a stability boundary; a thin margin is flagged as a risk to retire at FOAK. The record states the margin rather than asserting the design is 'stable', because stability is a boundary the machine must be shown to respect, not a property claimed by fiat.

title: The Density-Limit Benchmark
lede: The breeder's operating density is compared to the Greenwald limit, an empirical density ceiling above which tokamaks tend to disrupt.
body: Tokamaks show an empirical maximum line-averaged density, above which the plasma tends to disrupt. The standard reference is the Greenwald density limit, which rises with plasma current and falls with plasma size. Fusion power benefits from high density, so a design must sit at a defensible fraction of this limit, not beyond it.

# Greenwald density limit
# n_GW[1e20 m^-3] = Ip[MA] / (pi * a[m]^2)
# Operating at a fraction f_GW = n / n_GW, typically <= ~1.
# Design input: Ip = 9.66 MA. The benchmark reports f_GW for the
# design density and flags any point approaching unity.

Because the Greenwald limit rises with plasma current, the breeder's 9.66 MA supports a higher absolute density before the limit bites. The benchmark reports the Greenwald fraction f_GW at the design point; a value comfortably below one indicates headroom, while a value near one is recorded as an operating risk.

Density, confinement, and beta are not independent knobs. The record evaluates them together so that a design point does not satisfy each limit in isolation while violating a joint operating boundary. Cross-checking the coupled constraints is part of the sensitivity analysis.

The Greenwald limit is empirical, not a hard law of nature, and some machines exceed it under particular conditions. The breeder record does not lean on such exceptions: it targets a defensible fraction below one and treats any operating point that would rely on beating the empirical limit as a risk to retire at FOAK rather than a capability to assume in design.

title: The Bootstrap-Current Benchmark
lede: The self-generated bootstrap current is estimated with neoclassical theory and cross-checked against the spherical-tokamak record, because low aspect ratio favors a high bootstrap fraction.
body: Part of a tokamak's plasma current arises from the plasma's own pressure gradient — the bootstrap current. A high bootstrap fraction reduces the external current drive a steady machine must supply. Low-aspect-ratio spherical tokamaks favor a high bootstrap fraction, which is one reason the breeder (Hyperion) adopts the spherical geometry.

The bootstrap fraction is computed from neoclassical theory using the design pressure and current profiles, then compared to the fractions observed in NSTX/MAST-class experiments at similar aspect ratio. Agreement between theory and the ST database raises confidence; a discrepancy is flagged for FOAK measurement.
Why it matters for the gates

The bootstrap fraction feeds directly into whether the plasma current of 9.66 MA can be sustained without excessive recirculating power, which in turn affects the whole gain picture. The record reports the fraction with its uncertainty rather than assuming an optimistic value, and treats confirmation of the profile as a FOAK objective.

An optimistic bootstrap assumption is a common way a steady-state design flatters itself: overstate the self-driven fraction and the external current-drive burden shrinks on paper. The breeder analysis guards against this by carrying the neoclassical estimate with its interval and by refusing to credit a bootstrap fraction the ST database does not support at the design profiles.

title: The Neutron-Yield Benchmark
lede: The 14 MeV neutron source rate implied by 85.0 MW of D-T fusion power is cross-checked against first-principles reaction kinematics before any breeding or activation is computed.
body: From fusion power to neutron rate

The breeder's products — tritium, helium-3, and materials irradiation — all flow from one quantity: the rate of 14.1 MeV neutrons the plasma emits. That rate is fixed by the fusion power once the reaction is specified, so it is the first thing to benchmark. Each D-T reaction releases 17.6 MeV, of which 14.1 MeV is carried by the neutron.

# Neutron source rate from D-T fusion power
E_dt_MeV = 17.6          # energy per D-T reaction
E_n_MeV  = 14.1          # carried by the neutron
P_fus_MW = 85.0          # frozen design fusion power
MeV_to_J = 1.602e-13
reactions_per_s = (P_fus_MW*1e6) / (E_dt_MeV*MeV_to_J)
neutrons_per_s  = reactions_per_s   # one 14.1 MeV n per reaction
# ~3.1e19 neutrons/s -> feeds the breeding and activation analyses

The neutron rate looks like a trivial division, and that is exactly why it is worth pinning: every downstream product number multiplies it, so an error here would propagate everywhere. Benchmarking the source rate against reaction kinematics isolates a single, checkable step from the more model-dependent breeding and activation estimates that follow.
What it does not yet include

The source rate is the ceiling, not the yield. How many of those neutrons breed tritium depends on blanket coverage and the tritium breeding ratio, which is where the local-vs-net reconciliation enters. The neutron-yield benchmark deliberately stops at the source term.

title: The Tritium Breeding Ratio Open Question
lede: The breeder treats the tritium breeding ratio as a design lever across 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8; whether the 1.8 target survives realistic blanket geometry is an open reconciliation.
body: A lever, studied at three values

The tritium breeding ratio (TBR) is the number of tritium atoms bred per tritium atom burned. A D-T machine that consumes its own fuel must breed at least as much as it burns plus losses, so TBR above one is necessary for self-sufficiency. The breeder (Hyperion) record does not assert a single TBR; it studies the machine as a lever across 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8.

Why 1.8 is a target, not a claim

A local TBR computed for an idealized, fully surrounding blanket is optimistic. A real machine has ports, heating penetrations, diagnostic lines, and structural gaps that no breeding blanket covers, plus process losses in the fuel cycle. The gap between the idealized local figure and the net figure a real machine achieves is the open reconciliation. At the 1.8 target it is stated as unresolved.

Closing the question means a neutronics model with realistic geometry, validated against the neutronics benchmarks, that reproduces a net TBR meeting the target. Until that model exists and FOAK measurements confirm it, tritium self-sufficiency remains a design target rather than a demonstrated property.

title: Local vs Net Tritium Breeding Ratio
lede: An idealized local breeding ratio overstates what a real blanket delivers; the breeder record keeps the local-vs-net gap open at the 1.8 target rather than reporting a single number.
body: 'Tritium breeding ratio' names two things that are easy to conflate. The local TBR is what a patch of ideal blanket breeds per incident neutron, extrapolated as if the whole plasma were wrapped in that patch. The net TBR is what the actual machine breeds once real geometry, coverage, and losses are counted. The net figure is always lower.

For the target TBR of 1.8, the reconciliation between local and net is recorded as open. The record does not claim the net figure reaches 1.8; it states that whether it does is unresolved and depends on a realistic-geometry neutronics analysis still being matured. This is one of the breeder's named honest gates and appears in the contradictions register.

The practical consequence is that no single TBR number should be quoted as 'the' breeding ratio of the machine. A local figure describes an idealized blanket; a net figure describes the machine; and at the 1.8 target the second is not yet established. title: Tritium Self-Sufficiency Is Not Yet Proven
lede: A D-T machine must breed more tritium than it consumes; for the breeder this closure is a design target the record explicitly labels as unproven.
body: Tritium does not exist in useful natural quantity and decays with a 12.3-year half-life. A D-T fusion machine must therefore breed its own. Self-sufficiency is the condition that tritium bred, over a period, exceeds tritium burned plus tritium lost to decay and to processing. The breeder (Hyperion) is designed toward this closure; it has not demonstrated it.

# Tritium balance (schematic closure condition)
# bred >= burned + decay_losses + process_losses + startup_holdup
# net_TBR = bred / burned  must exceed 1 with margin for the losses.
# Status: target net TBR toward 1.8; local-vs-net gap OPEN;
#         closure is a DESIGN TARGET, not a demonstrated result.
Why it is honest to flag this

Every D-T fusion concept faces this problem, and a program that does not name it is hiding its hardest fuel-cycle question. The breeder record states plainly that self-sufficiency is unproven, that it depends on resolving the local-vs-net TBR, and that a startup tritium inventory and fuel-cycle losses must be counted in the balance, not assumed away.

Proof requires a validated net-TBR analysis at realistic geometry followed by FOAK operation measuring the actual tritium accounting. Until both exist, the correct statement is that the machine is designed to be self-sufficient, and whether it is remains to be shown.

Startup is a distinct part of the problem that is easy to overlook. A breeder cannot breed before it operates, so a first inventory of tritium must come from elsewhere to begin, and the fuel cycle must then overtake burn and losses to become self-supporting. The record counts this startup holdup in the balance rather than presenting self-sufficiency as a property the machine possesses from the first shot.

title: The Center-Post Lifetime Gate
lede: A compact spherical tokamak puts its center stack in the harshest neutron field; the breeder record carries a limited-lifetime note (order 0.01 full-power-years) as a stated engineering constraint.
body: The spherical geometry that gives the breeder (Hyperion) its high-beta, high-bootstrap advantages also forces the center stack into a small radius, close to the plasma, in an intense 14 MeV neutron flux. Neutron damage accumulates in the center-post conductor and structure, and that sets a replacement interval. The record states this as an engineering gate, not a solved problem.

title: Negative Triangularity: What Is and Is Not Settled
lede: The breeder adopts negative triangularity (delta -0.30) for edge and exhaust reasons; the record separates the well-motivated choice from the parts that FOAK must still confirm.
body: Most tokamaks run positive triangularity, a D-shaped cross section with the corners pointing toward the center column. The breeder (Hyperion) runs negative triangularity, delta -0.30 — the D bows outward. The motivation is edge and exhaust behavior: negative triangularity is associated with a benign edge that avoids certain large edge instabilities.

The choice draws on experiments at conventional aspect ratio that observed favorable edge behavior with negative triangularity. The breeder record cites that basis and includes the shape in its equilibrium and stability analyses among the 81.
Negative triangularity at low aspect ratio (A 2.5) is far less explored than at conventional aspect ratio.
The interaction of the outward-bowed edge with the breeder's exhaust and divertor loading.
Confinement at negative triangularity in this regime, where the ST database is thin.
Whether the equilibrium is as controllable in hardware as in simulation.

The record's position is that the shape is a reasoned design choice with a real experimental basis, and that its behavior in this specific low-aspect-ratio, D-T breeding context is a simulation result to be confirmed, not an established fact.

title: Pre-Registered, Falsifiable Predictions
lede: Before FOAK operates, the breeder record commits in writing to specific measurable outcomes and the values that would refute the design, so success cannot be redefined after the fact.
body: A prediction registered after data is collected can always be shaped to fit. The breeder (Hyperion) program instead pre-registers predictions: it states, before first-of-a-kind operation, what the machine should measure and — crucially — what result would count as a failure. The commitments live in the versioned, DOI-stamped record, so their date is fixed.

A prediction without a falsifier is not a test. For every pre-registered claim, the record names the observation that would refute it. Confinement: a predicted confinement time and the value below which the gain case fails.
Breeding: a predicted net TBR band and the value below which self-sufficiency is refuted.
Neutron spectrum: a predicted 14 MeV peak and tolerance.
Magnet field: a predicted peak field and the tolerance on 16.84 T.
These are detailed on their own pages. The point of the overview is the discipline: the falsifiers are published before the data exists.

title: Pre-Registered Prediction: Confinement
lede: The breeder commits to a confinement-time prediction and states the threshold below which the Q_sci 3.076 gain case is refuted.
body: The breeder (Hyperion) gain figure, Q_sci 3.076 at 85.0 MW of fusion power, depends on the energy confinement time. The record pre-registers a predicted confinement time at the design point, derived from the transport model and cross-checked against the ST database and the ITER-basis scaling.

The commitment includes an explicit threshold: a measured confinement time below a stated fraction of the prediction refutes the gain case as designed. If FOAK confines that poorly, Q_sci 3.076 is not reachable at the design inputs, and the record will say the prediction failed rather than re-fitting the model to the disappointing number.

# Pre-registered confinement test (schematic)
tau_pred = TAU_E_DESIGN          # published before FOAK, DOI-stamped
tau_fail = 0.?? * tau_pred       # stated refuting threshold
def verdict(tau_meas):
    if tau_meas >= tau_pred:   return 'confirmed'
    if tau_meas <  tau_fail:   return 'REFUTED: gain case fails'
    return 'partial: design margin eroded, re-examine'

Naming the value that would prove the design wrong is what makes the confirming case meaningful. A prediction that no possible measurement could break carries no information. The confinement falsifier converts FOAK from a demonstration into a genuine test.

title: Pre-Registered Prediction: Tritium Breeding
lede: The breeder commits to a net-TBR band measurable at FOAK and names the value below which tritium self-sufficiency is refuted.
body: The breeder (Hyperion) studies TBR as a lever at 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8, with the local-vs-net gap open at the 1.8 target. The pre-registered prediction is a net TBR band that FOAK tritium accounting should measure, stated together with the realistic-geometry assumptions behind it.

The falsifier is a measured net TBR below the value required for self-sufficiency given the fuel-cycle losses. If FOAK breeds below that line, the record will report that tritium self-sufficiency at the design is refuted — not that the target was 'nearly' met. Because self-sufficiency is already flagged as unproven, this prediction is where that gate is put to the test.

# Pre-registered net-TBR test (schematic)
TBR_needed = 1.0 + losses_fraction   # closure with margin
def verdict(tbr_net_meas):
    if tbr_net_meas >= TBR_needed: return 'self-sufficiency supported'
    return 'REFUTED: net breeding below closure'
Honest about what FOAK can measure

FOAK first tritium near 2030 begins the accounting; a defensible net-TBR measurement requires integrated operation over time, not a single shot. The prediction therefore specifies the operating interval over which the tritium balance is to be judged, so the falsifier is testable and not evaded by short runs.

title: Pre-Registered Prediction: Neutron Spectrum
lede: The breeder predicts a 14.1 MeV D-T neutron peak with a stated tolerance, giving a sharp, early test of whether the plasma burns as modeled.
body: D-T fusion emits a characteristic neutron at 14.1 MeV. The breeder (Hyperion) pre-registers the predicted neutron energy spectrum at representative detector locations: a dominant 14.1 MeV peak, its expected broadening from plasma temperature, and the softened tail from neutrons scattered in the blanket and structure.

A measured peak displaced from 14.1 MeV beyond the stated tolerance, or a peak-to-tail ratio outside the predicted band, refutes the neutronics model as configured. Because the whole product chain multiplies the neutron source rate, an early spectrum measurement is a low-cost, high-information check that the plasma and blanket behave as simulated.

The neutron spectrum can be measured early and does not require long integrated operation. It tests the reaction identity, the plasma temperature, and the surrounding geometry at once, and it validates the model that the harder breeding measurement depends on. It is among the first predictions FOAK can decisively confirm or break.

Because it is early and cheap, the spectrum test also functions as a tripwire: a spectrum that disagrees with prediction signals that something upstream — the reaction mix, the temperature, or the geometry model — is wrong before the program has committed to the far more expensive breeding campaign. Catching a foundational error at the spectrum stage is far preferable to discovering it only in the tritium accounting.

title: Pre-Registered Prediction: Magnet Field
lede: The breeder predicts a peak field of 16.84 T with 8 T on-axis and states the tolerance a magnetic measurement must meet, testing the magnet design directly.
body: The breeder (Hyperion) relies on high-temperature-superconducting magnets to produce a peak field of 16.84 T at the conductor and 8 T on-axis at the plasma. These fields are prerequisites for the plasma current of 9.66 MA and the confinement behind Q_sci 3.076. The record pre-registers the predicted field values and profile.

A measured on-axis field below 8 T beyond tolerance, or a peak conductor field that cannot reach 16.84 T without exceeding the magnet's stress or quench limits, refutes the magnet operating point as designed. This is a comparatively direct test: the field is measurable with standard magnetic diagnostics early in commissioning, before plasma operation.

# Pre-registered field test (schematic)
B_axis_pred = 8.0     # T on-axis
B_peak_pred = 16.84   # T at conductor
def verdict(B_axis, B_peak, tol=0.05):
    ok = (abs(B_axis-B_axis_pred) <= tol*B_axis_pred and
          B_peak <= B_peak_pred*(1+tol))
    return 'field confirmed' if ok else 'REFUTED: magnet point'

Because magnet fields can be verified before first plasma, this prediction is among the earliest to resolve. Confirming it de-risks a large block of downstream physics that assumes the design field; failing it forces a redesign before plasma operation rather than after.

Reproduction checks that the computation is faithful — that the published numbers follow from the inputs and code. It does not, and cannot, validate against a machine that has not been built. title: The Reproduction Environment
lede: The breeder analyses pin their software environment — interpreter, libraries, and versions — so a rerun is not silently changed by whatever a reproducer happens to have installed.
body: Pinning what the code runs on

A number can change because the code changed, or because the environment underneath it changed — a different library version, a different floating-point path, a different platform. To make reproduction meaningful, the breeder (Hyperion) analyses pin the environment as tightly as the code.
Every library dependency is pinned to an exact version.
Random seeds are recorded for any stochastic step.
A container or lockfile captures the whole environment for one-command rebuild.

# Environment is captured, not assumed
# - lockfile pins exact dependency versions
# - container image freezes interpreter + libs + OS libs
# - each analysis records the seed it used
# Reproduce with the pinned environment, not your local one.

Even with pinned versions, different CPUs and math libraries can produce tiny floating-point differences. That is why reproduction is defined at two tiers: a Tier-1 byte-exact match where the environment is identical, and a Tier-2 within-tolerance match where it is not. Both are legitimate; the record states which tier a given analysis is expected to meet.

Pinned environments age: libraries are deprecated, platforms move on. The container approach mitigates this by freezing the whole stack, and the versioned deposit means an old environment specification remains retrievable alongside the numbers it produced.

lede: The breeder record accepts two levels of reproduction — a byte-for-byte match in an identical environment, and a numerically-close match across platforms — and states which each analysis targets.
body: 'I reproduced it' can mean two different things, and conflating them causes needless disputes. The breeder (Hyperion) record defines both explicitly so a reproducer knows which bar to clear.

In the pinned container, on a compatible platform, an output file should match the published file bit for bit; its checksum should be identical. This is the strongest form of reproduction and is expected for deterministic analyses run in the reference environment.

On a different platform or math library, floating-point results can differ in the last digits. Tier 2 accepts a match within a stated numerical tolerance rather than bit-for-bit. The tolerance is published per analysis, so 'close enough' is a defined number, not a judgment call.
A Tier-2 pass with a Tier-1 failure is normal across platforms and does not indicate an error. A Tier-2 failure does, and is a reportable discrepancy.

Separating the tiers prevents a common and pointless argument. Without the distinction, a reproducer on different hardware sees last-digit differences, concludes the record is wrong, and reports a non-existent error; or an author dismisses a genuine discrepancy as mere floating-point noise. Publishing a per-analysis tolerance settles which reading is correct before the dispute starts, because 'close enough' is a number in the deposit rather than a matter of opinion.

body: Released so it can be checked

Reproduction is impossible without the code that turns inputs into outputs. The breeder (Hyperion) analysis code is released under an open license so a third party can read it, run it, and audit it. The license terms are stated in the deposit and repository so there is no ambiguity about permitted use.
The analysis and post-processing code that produces the published figures.

The expected outputs and per-analysis tolerances.

Code is released under a permissive open-source license so it can be reused and independently verified; the exact license text ships with the repository. title: Data Availability Statement
lede: The inputs, intermediate data, and outputs behind the breeder numbers are deposited or pointed to, and their provenance is stated; nothing load-bearing is withheld.
body: A validation record must say where its data comes from and where a reader can get it. For the breeder (Hyperion), the frozen inputs, the analysis outputs, and the checksums that bind them are deposited on Zenodo with the manuscript. External reference data — such as the empirical scalings used for benchmarking — is cited to its original source.
Design inputs and frozen parameters: in the deposit.
Analysis outputs and figures: in the deposit, with checksums.

title: How Uncertainty Is Quantified
lede: Breeder results are reported with uncertainties, not as point values; this page describes how input uncertainty is propagated to every headline number.
body: A number without an uncertainty is incomplete

The breeder (Hyperion) headline figures — Q_sci 3.076, 85.0 MW, and the product yields — are the central estimates of distributions, not exact truths. Each rests on inputs that carry uncertainty: confinement scaling coefficients, profile assumptions, cross-sections, and geometry. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) propagates those input uncertainties through the analyses to bracket the outputs.

# Monte-Carlo style propagation (schematic)
import numpy as np
def propagate(model, priors, N=10000):
    samples = [model(**draw(priors)) for _ in range(N)]
    return np.mean(samples), np.percentile(samples,[5,95])
# Reported: central value + a stated confidence interval,
# not a bare point estimate.
Scaling-law coefficient uncertainty from the empirical fits.
Profile and boundary assumptions varied across plausible ranges.
Nuclear-data uncertainty in the neutronics and breeding analyses.
Geometry tolerances where they affect coverage.

Where an interval is wide, the record says so rather than quoting only the optimistic edge. The TBR lever at 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8 is itself a UQ posture: the record spans the range instead of committing to a single breeding number, because the underlying uncertainty is real. Sensitivity — which inputs drive the spread — is covered in the sensitivity analysis.

title: Verification vs Validation
lede: Verification asks whether the code solves the equations right; validation asks whether the equations describe the machine. The breeder is verified in places and awaits hardware validation everywhere.
body: 'V and V' names two distinct checks that are easy to blur. Verification: does the code correctly solve the mathematical model it claims to? Validation: does that model correctly describe physical reality? The breeder (Hyperion) record keeps them separate because the honest status differs sharply between them.

Verification: partly done, and doable now

Verification does not need a machine. It uses techniques like the method of manufactured solutions, convergence studies, and conservation checks. The breeder record includes such checks for its solvers and reports them as one of the things reproduction can confirm today.

Validation requires comparing model output to measurement from the actual system. Because the breeder is not built, its models are not yet validated against hardware. Benchmarking against other machines' data provides partial, indirect validation for shared physics, but the specific integrated breeder design is validated only when FOAK measures it near 2030.
The clean statement: verification is in progress and reproducible; validation is pending, and no page claims otherwise. See solver verification.

The words are worth guarding because the field routinely blurs them. A press statement that a code is 'validated' when it has only been verified overstates what is known by a wide margin, and a reader cannot recover the difference from the word alone. The breeder record uses 'validated' only for a comparison against hardware, which means today it uses the word for nothing, and says so.

title: The Automated verify() Firewall
lede: An automated check regenerates the breeder pages from the frozen record and refuses to publish if any number, DOI, or claim disagrees with canon.
body: A large public record drifts if humans retype numbers. The breeder (Hyperion) site is generated from the frozen record and passes an automated verify() check before publishing. If a page states a fusion power other than 85.0 MW, a gain other than 3.076, or a DOI that does not resolve, the check fails and the build stops.

def verify(pages, canon):
    for p in pages:
        assert canon['q_sci'] in text(p) or 'q_sci' not in topic(p)
        assert no_economics(p)          # no prices, cost, or rate figures
        assert dois_resolve(p)          # 21746157 / 21795620
        assert gates_not_softened(p)    # honest gates intact
    return 'CLEAN'
Frozen canon numbers: Q_sci 3.076, 85.0 MW, 9.66 MA, 16.84 T / 8 T on-axis, delta -0.30.
The economics firewall: no prices, costs, or valuations anywhere.
The honest gates: the TBR reconciliation and center-post note are not silently removed.
Why this is a validation tool

Consistency is a precondition for reproducibility. If the public text and the underlying record disagree, a reproducer cannot know which to trust. The verify() firewall makes the two agree by construction, so the number a reader sees is the number the analysis produced.

title: Solver Verification by Manufactured Solutions
lede: The breeder's numerical solvers are verified with the method of manufactured solutions and convergence studies — checks that need no machine and can be reproduced today.
body: Checking the solver against known answers

Before trusting a solver on a problem with no known answer, you check it on problems that do. The method of manufactured solutions (MMS) constructs an exact solution by design, inserts the matching source term into the equations, and confirms the solver recovers it at the expected order of accuracy. The breeder (Hyperion) code applies MMS to its core solvers.

# Method of manufactured solutions (schematic)
# 1. Pick an exact u*(x): e.g. u* = sin(pi x)
# 2. Insert into operator L: compute forcing f = L[u*]
# 3. Solve L[u]=f numerically -> u_h
# 4. error = ||u_h - u*||; refine grid; check order p:
#    error ~ C * h^p  (p should match the scheme's design order)
Convergence: refining the grid should shrink error at the scheme's design order; a wrong order signals a bug.
Conservation: quantities that should be conserved (particles, energy) must not drift.
Limiting cases: the solver must reproduce known analytic limits.

Passing MMS means the code solves its equations correctly. It says nothing about whether those equations describe a real breeder plasma — that is validation, which awaits FOAK. But verification is a real, reproducible result available now, and it is part of what an independent reproducer can confirm from the deposit.

The two also fail independently. A perfectly verified code can encode a wrong physical model and confidently produce wrong answers; a sound model can be undone by a coding error a verification suite would catch. Because the breeder is verified in places but validated nowhere in hardware, the honest present-tense status is that the arithmetic can be trusted to the extent it has been verified, and the physics awaits the machine.

title: Validating the Equilibrium Reconstruction
lede: The breeder's magnetic equilibrium — its negative-triangularity shape at 9.66 MA — is solved and cross-checked, with the caveat that low-aspect-ratio validation data is limited.
body: Everything downstream depends on the plasma's magnetic equilibrium: the shape, the current distribution, and the field. The breeder (Hyperion) equilibrium is a strongly shaped, negative-triangularity (delta -0.30) configuration at 9.66 MA and 8 T on-axis. The reconstruction is solved by a Grad-Shafranov solver and checked for self-consistency.

Solver verification via MMS and convergence, as above.
Cross-comparison against an independent equilibrium code where possible.
Consistency with the prescribed current and pressure profiles.

Solving an equilibrium correctly is verification; confirming it matches a real plasma is validation. Negative triangularity at low aspect ratio is thinly represented in existing data, so the equilibrium's fidelity to a real breeder plasma is a FOAK-era question. The field prediction that the equilibrium implies is pre-registered so it can be tested directly.

A subtle risk with strongly shaped equilibria is that a solver can converge to a mathematically valid solution that a real control system cannot hold. The record therefore treats controllability of the negative-triangularity shape as a separate question from existence of the equilibrium, and defers the controllability claim to FOAK rather than inferring it from a converged solve.

title: Validating the Transport Model
lede: The transport model behind the breeder's confinement and gain is the least certain link; the record benchmarks it against other machines and pre-registers its FOAK test.
body: The softest link in the chain

Turbulent transport sets the energy confinement time, and confinement sets the gain. Transport is also the hardest fusion physics to predict from first principles, so it is the breeder (Hyperion) model most in need of validation. The record treats it accordingly: it does not overstate confidence in the confinement prediction behind Q_sci 3.076.

Comparison of the transport model against experimental confinement where geometry overlaps.
Propagating transport-model uncertainty into the reported gain interval.

If any single model is going to be surprised by hardware, transport is the candidate. Stating that plainly — and pre-registering the confinement falsifier — is more credible than presenting the confinement number as settled. FOAK is the arbiter.

It is worth being precise about what a transport disagreement would and would not overturn. A confinement shortfall would erode or break the Q_sci 3.076 case, but it would not touch the neutron kinematics or the measured field; those rest on firmer ground. Isolating the soft link keeps a possible surprise contained to the claims that actually depend on it, rather than casting doubt across the whole record.

lede: The neutron transport and activation model underpins every product number; its accuracy is bounded by nuclear-data uncertainty, which the record propagates rather than ignores.

The breeder (Hyperion) product figures — near 4 kg/yr tritium class and 1.97 kg/yr helium-3 — are outputs of this model, so its validation is central.

Neutronics accuracy is bounded below by the uncertainty in evaluated cross-sections, which is real and not reducible by better geometry alone. The record reports product yields with intervals that include this floor. The step where model geometry matters most — realistic blanket coverage — feeds directly into the local-vs-net TBR gate, which is why that gate is open.

The neutronics model therefore sits at the junction of two different uncertainty types: an irreducible nuclear-data floor that better geometry cannot remove, and a geometry-and-coverage uncertainty that a more faithful model can reduce. The record keeps them distinct so a reader knows which part of a product-yield interval could tighten with more work and which part is set by the state of evaluated nuclear data.

title: Validating the Surrogate Models
lede: Fast surrogate models stand in for expensive simulations during design exploration; the record validates each surrogate against the full model it replaces and states its error.
body: Exploring a design space requires thousands of evaluations, which the full physics codes cannot supply quickly. Surrogate models — fast approximations trained on full-model runs — fill that gap for the breeder (Hyperion). A surrogate is only trustworthy inside the region it was trained on and to the accuracy it was validated at, and the record states both.

# Surrogate validation (schematic)
# 1. Train surrogate s(x) on full-model samples {x_i, f(x_i)}
# 2. Hold out test points not used in training
# 3. Report error: max & RMS |s(x)-f(x)| on held-out set
# 4. Record the valid input domain; refuse extrapolation beyond it
Held-out test error, not training error, defines a surrogate's accuracy.
The valid input domain is stated; extrapolation is flagged, not silent.
Headline results are confirmed on the full model, not left to the surrogate.
Surrogate uncertainty is included in the reported intervals.

Surrogates accelerate exploration; they do not certify results. Every quantity that appears in the record's headline claims is checked against the full model it approximates. A surrogate that disagrees with its parent model outside tolerance is a bug to fix, and its domain of validity is part of the uncertainty budget.

title: What FOAK First Tritium Will Not Prove
lede: First-of-a-kind first tritium is a milestone, not a finish line; it will not prove net-TBR self-sufficiency, long-run center-post survival, or fleet-scale performance.
body: When FOAK breeds its first tritium near 2030, it will be tempting to treat the whole design as validated. The breeder (Hyperion) record marks the boundaries in advance so the milestone is not over-read.
Not net self-sufficiency: first tritium shows the chain works, not that net breeding exceeds burn plus losses over time. Net TBR requires sustained accounting.
Not the local-vs-net TBR closure at 1.8: that reconciliation remains open until a realistic-geometry measurement resolves it.
Not center-post longevity: the ~0.01 fpy lifetime note is about accumulated damage over full-power-years, which early operation cannot reach.
Not fleet performance: one FOAK machine says little about NOAK and BOAK learning, which follow.
Not net electric power: the breeder is a foundry; no net-gain claim is made before or at FOAK.

Programs lose credibility by letting a real milestone be reported as more than it is. Stating the limits before the event means the eventual claims match what was promised. The honest gates remain gates until the specific measurement that closes each one is made.

There is a positive reason to draw these limits so firmly. A milestone that is reported for exactly what it is can be believed the next time; a milestone inflated into more than it showed spends credibility the program will need later. By fixing in advance what first tritium does and does not settle, the record makes its eventual FOAK claims easy to check against what was promised here.

lede: Open deposit is the floor, not the ceiling; the breeder work is offered to external peer review, and the record distinguishes deposited-and-citable from peer-reviewed.

title: The Open-Science Principles
lede: The breeder record follows a small set of commitments — open data, open code, stated uncertainty, named gates, and permanent citability — that together define its posture.
body: The breeder (Hyperion) program's open-science posture is not a slogan; it is a set of concrete commitments that each map to a mechanism elsewhere in this record.
Open data: inputs and outputs are deposited with checksums (data availability).
Open code: analysis code is released under an open license (code availability).
Reproducibility: pinned environments and two-tier reproduction (reproduction guide).
Stated uncertainty: results carry intervals, not just point values (UQ method).
Named gates: the open questions are published, not hidden (honest gates).
Pre-registration: falsifiers published before the data (pre-registration).
No economics: the public record carries no prices, costs, or valuations.

Each commitment also has a failure mode that would expose it: a broken checksum defeats open data, an unpinned dependency defeats reproducibility, a removed gate defeats honesty, and an overwritten deposit defeats permanence. title: A Glossary of Validation Terms
lede: Plain definitions of the validation and open-science terms used across the breeder record, so a reader is never guessing what a word means.
body: The breeder (Hyperion) record uses several terms in specific technical senses. This glossary fixes them so the pages read the same way to everyone.
Verification: confirming the code solves its equations correctly (no machine needed).
Validation: confirming the equations describe the real machine (needs hardware).
Reproducibility: a third party obtaining the same output from the same inputs and code.
Tier-1 reproduction: a byte-exact match in the reference environment.
Tier-2 reproduction: a within-tolerance match across environments.
TBR (tritium breeding ratio): tritium bred per tritium burned; local vs net distinguished.
Local TBR: idealized breeding for full-coverage blanket; optimistic.
Net TBR: breeding after real coverage, penetrations, and losses.
Pre-registration: publishing a prediction and its falsifier before the data exists.
Falsifier: the observation that would prove a prediction wrong.
UQ (uncertainty quantification): propagating input uncertainty to output intervals.
Sensitivity: how strongly an output responds to a given input.
Honest gate: a named open question the record has not closed.
FOAK / NOAK / BOAK: first-, next-, and best-of-a-kind machines in the build sequence.
Full-power-year (fpy): one year of operation at full power, the unit for damage lifetimes.
Concept DOI / version DOI: identifiers for the work in general vs a specific deposit.

Why a glossary is a validation tool

Ambiguous language hides disagreement. When 'reproduced' or 'validated' means one thing to the author and another to the reader, a claim can seem stronger than it is. Fixing the definitions is part of keeping the record honest. The distinctions that carry the most weight are verification versus validation and local versus net TBR: in each pair the two terms sound interchangeable and are not, and most over-claims in fusion communication come from sliding between them. The record uses the stricter member of each pair as its default.

title: The Contradictions Register
lede: Where the breeder record contains an unresolved tension or an open reconciliation, it is listed here rather than smoothed over, so a reader sees the seams.
body: No large design study is perfectly self-consistent while its physics is still maturing. The breeder (Hyperion) record keeps a register of the tensions it has not resolved, so they are visible in one place instead of being discovered by a careful reader as apparent inconsistencies.

How an item enters and leaves
Enters when reproduction, review, or internal analysis finds an unresolved tension.
Carries a plain-language statement and a current status.
Leaves only when a specific analysis or FOAK measurement closes it — with the closing evidence cited.
A closed item is archived, not deleted, so the history is preserved.

A register of contradictions is the opposite of a marketing document, and that is the point. It tells a reader precisely where the design is still soft, which is the information a serious reviewer most wants. Each item links to its own page — the TBR reconciliation and the center-post gate among them — where the tension is described in full.

The register is deliberately not a bug tracker of typos; it lists tensions that could change a conclusion. That threshold keeps it short and meaningful. A reader who wants the fastest honest read of where the breeder design is still soft can start here and follow the links, rather than reconstructing the open questions from scattered caveats across the rest of the record.

title: The Digital Twin as a Validation Instrument
lede: The interactive model of the breeder is more than a visualization; it is the framework that will ingest FOAK data and test the pre-registered predictions in place.
body: Today the breeder (Hyperion) digital twin is a design-and-simulation model: it embodies the equilibrium, the neutron budget, and the product chain at the frozen design point. Its longer purpose is validation. As FOAK produces data near 2030, the same framework becomes the place where prediction meets measurement.

Holds the pre-registered predictions and their falsifiers in executable form.
Ingests hardware measurements and compares them to prediction automatically.
Flags a refuted prediction rather than re-fitting to the new data.
Keeps the comparison reproducible: the same inputs give the same verdict.

A digital twin does not validate itself. Until FOAK supplies measurement, the twin is a consistent simulation, not a validated one — the same status as the rest of the record. Its value is that it makes the eventual validation systematic: every pre-registered prediction has a defined home where it will be confirmed or broken, and the verdict is computed, not asserted.

The twin also protects against a quiet failure mode of comparison: moving the goalposts after the data arrives. Because the predictions and their falsifiers are already encoded and DOI-stamped, the twin evaluates measurement against the commitment as written, and a refuted prediction is recorded as refuted. The instrument's discipline is precisely that it cannot be talked out of an unfavorable verdict.
